concepts.title: Levels and Global Patterns of Biodiversity
concepts.definition: Biodiversity is expressed at three levels: genetic diversity (like more than a thousand rice varieties in India), species diversity (over 1.5 million plant and animal species described so far) and ecological diversity (from deserts to mangroves), with the Amazonian rainforest holding the greatest biodiversity on earth.
concepts.key_idea: For every 10 square kilometres of Amazonian forest there are probably more kinds of plants and animals than in the whole of Europe, which is why conserving forest area matters more than raw species counts.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo113.txt genetic-species-ecological diversity sections and Amazon estimate

how do ecologists estimate total species numbers

solution_steps.explain: genes, species and ecosystems form the three-tier measure of biodiversity
1.5 million described species sit far below ecologist estimates of the true total
the Amazon rainforest is the benchmark of global species richness

concepts.title: Species-Area Relationship
concepts.definition: Species richness S rises with explored area A and on a log scale is a straight line, log S = log C + Z log A; the regression slope Z lies in the range 0.1 to 0.2 for ordinary regional analyses but steepens to 0.6 to 1.2 when whole continents are compared.
concepts.key_idea: The gap between the shallow regional slopes and the steep continental slopes shows that species accumulation accelerates with scale, which is why conserving large continuous habitats matters.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo113.txt species-area equation and slope ranges (0.1-0.2, 0.6-1.2)

solution_steps.action: take the two reported slope bands
solution_steps.explain: regional slopes reach 0.2 and continental slopes start at 0.6

solution_steps.action: subtract the shallow upper bound from the steep lower bound
solution_steps.explain: the gap shows how much steeper continental accumulation is

concepts.title: Importance and the Rivet Popper Hypothesis
concepts.definition: Ecologists ask why we should save species; the rivet popper hypothesis of Paul Ehrlich compares an ecosystem to an aeroplane where popping rivets (extinctions) may seem harmless until a critical rivet fails and the plane (ecosystem function) crashes.
concepts.key_idea: Species diversity is insurance for ecosystem services: every lost rivet raises the chance that the next extinction is the fatal one.
question_patterns: state the rivet popper hypothesis in Ehrlich's analogy
how does the airplane analogy support conservation
distinguish the rivet popper view from a mere species-count view
why might losing a key-stone rivet be catastrophic
link biodiversity loss to ecosystem services
what does the hypothesis imply for habitat destruction

solution_steps.explain: airplane equals ecosystem, rivets equal species, popping equals extinction
the last rivet does the damage, so cumulative loss is nonlinear
productivity, pollination and climate buffers degrade along with the rivets

concepts.title: In-situ and Ex-situ Conservation
concepts.definition: Conservation strategies split into in-situ protection in natural habitats (biodiversity hotspots, sacred groves, biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries) and ex-situ preservation off-site (zoological parks, tissue culture and seed banks), with hotspots defined by high endemism and exceptional threat.
concepts.key_idea: India counts three biodiversity hotspots - the Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Eastern Himalaya - and sacred groves show how culture protected forests before statutes did.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebo113.txt hotspot criteria, sacred groves and ex-situ techniques sections
question_patterns: differentiate in-situ and ex-situ conservation with examples

solution_steps.explain: hotspots, parks and sacred groves stay in habitat; zoos and seed banks remove it
high endemicity plus high threat level flags a region for priority action
the three Indian hotspots concentrate national conservation funding

worked_examples.question_pattern: Sort the following into in-situ and ex-situ conservation: sacred grove, seed bank, national park, zoological park, tissue culture, biosphere reserve.

solution_template.explain: sacred grove, national park and biosphere reserve protect habitats in place
seed bank, tissue culture and zoological park conserve organisms off-site
in-situ keeps evolutionary processes running; ex-situ is a stopgap against total loss

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the rivet popper hypothesis and one conservation decision it supports.

solution_template.explain: extinctions are rivets popped from an aeroplane hull
